\chapter{Seasons}
\label{ch:ml-seasons}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name Malayalam's four seasons, including the monsoon that sits at the centre of the year.}

Say vēnalkkālam, mazhakkālam and śaithyakālam as native compounds, then vasanthakālam as the shared Sanskrit loan.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{വസന്തകാലം} \ml{വേനൽക്കാലം} \ml{മഴക്കാലം} \ml{ശൈത്യകാലം}]{\ml{വസന്തകാലം}, \ml{വേനൽ}, \ml{മഴ}, \ml{ശൈത്യം} — the same pattern as Tamil}

\label{lesson:ML-C14-kaalangal}



\begin{quote}
Malayalam's season words follow the very same recipe as Tamil's — native words for what a season \emph{feels like}, plus one shared Sanskrit loan for spring.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Malayalam} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{വസന്തകാലം}} (\emph{vasanthakaalam}) & \textquotedblleft{}spring\textquotedblright{} & \emph{vasantham} — the same \textbf{Sanskrit} loan as Tamil \\
\textbf{\ml{വേനൽക്കാലം}} (\emph{venalkkaalam}) & \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\ml{വേനൽ}} \emph{venal}, native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{kodai}'s role \\
\textbf{\ml{മഴക്കാലം}} (\emph{mazhakkaalam}) & \textquotedblleft{}rainy season\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{\ml{മഴ}} \emph{mazha}, native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{mazhai} closely \\
\textbf{\ml{ശൈത്യകാലം}} (\emph{śaithyakaalam}) & \textquotedblleft{}winter/cold season\textquotedblright{} & \emph{śaithya} — this one leans more \textbf{Sanskrit-flavored} than Tamil's native \emph{kulir} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one shares the ending \textbf{‑\ml{കാലം}} (\emph{‑kaalam}, \textquotedblleft{}time/season\textquotedblright{}) — itself ultimately from Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{काल}} (\emph{kāla}), but assimilated so long ago that it functions as ordinary vocabulary, quite unlike a fresher loan like \emph{vasantham}.

\begin{culture}
As with Tamil, Kerala's actual climate is shaped far more by \textbf{\ml{മഴക്കാലം}} (\emph{mazhakkaalam}, \textquotedblleft{}the rains\textquotedblright{} — including Kerala's famous southwest monsoon) than by a clean four-way Western split. The rains aren't a footnote to \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}autumn\textquotedblright{} — they're their own major season, central to daily and agricultural life.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}venal\textquotedblright{} — summer heat — then \textquotedblleft{}kaalam,\textquotedblright{} season
  \item \textquotedblleft{}mazhakkaalam\textquotedblright{} — the rains, the real central season
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śaithyakaalam\textquotedblright{} — the cold season
  \item the shared loanword — \textquotedblleft{}vasanthakaalam,\textquotedblright{} spring, same as Tamil
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Malayalam season-words match Tamil's closely, and which is shared with Tamil as a Sanskrit loan? (\textbf{Venal/mazha} match Tamil's \emph{kodai/mazhai}; \textbf{vasanthakaalam} is the same Sanskrit loan as Tamil's \emph{vasantha kaalam}.) What's the real central season in Kerala's climate? (\textbf{Mazhakkaalam}, the rains/monsoon.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[llla]{\ml{ഴ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S118-letter-llla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ട} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഴ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഴ}} — \emph{llla}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{lll}, it is \textbf{llla}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \ml{ഴ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ആറ്} \ml{ഏഴ്} \ml{എട്ട്} \ml{ഒമ്പത്} \ml{പത്ത്}} — six to ten
  \item \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കൾ} \ml{ചൊവ്വ} \ml{ബുധൻ} \ml{വ്യാഴം} \ml{വെള്ളി} \ml{ശനി} \ml{ഞായർ}} — the seven weekdays
  \item \textbf{\ml{വസന്തകാലം} \ml{വേനൽക്കാലം} \ml{മഴക്കാലം} \ml{ശൈത്യകാലം}} — spring, summer, monsoon, winter
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \ml{ഴ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \ml{ഴ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \ml{ഴ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{നമസ്കാരം}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ml{ഴ} three times, saying \emph{llla} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \ml{ഴ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \ml{ഴ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{llla}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
